title: Review a singleton service that captures a scoped dependency
description: Problem: Review a singleton service that captures a scoped dependency. Solve this problem with multiple approaches and detailed explanations.

data.text: A singleton service constructor accepts a scoped DbContext or repository. Because the singleton is created once, it captures the first scoped instance and reuses it across all subsequent requests. The second request receives a DbContext that is already disposed, or worse, it sees stale data from the first request. This bug is silent in development and catastrophic in production.

items: Understand the three service lifetimes in ASP.NET Core: transient, scoped, and singleton
Learn why capturing a scoped dependency in a singleton constructor creates a hidden captive dependency
Identify runtime symptoms: ObjectDisposedException, cross-request data leakage, and incorrect audit trails
Apply factory patterns or IServiceScopeFactory to resolve scoped services safely

terms.definition: The container's rule for how long an instance lives: transient (new every time), scoped (one per request), or singleton (one per application).
A dependency that outlives its intended lifetime because a longer-lived service holds a reference to it.
A service that creates a new IServiceScope, giving you a fresh scoped container inside a singleton or background thread.
Entity Framework Core's unit-of-work. It is registered as scoped by default because it holds a database connection and change tracker that must not be shared across requests.

data.text: Captive dependencies violate the dependency inversion principle and create race conditions that are nearly impossible to reproduce in a single-threaded test. In production, under concurrent load, the singleton's captured DbContext is accessed from multiple requests simultaneously. Entity Framework Core is not thread-safe, so the result is intermittent crashes, corrupted queries, and data bleeding between users.

data.title: Captive dependency is a production time bomb
data.text: The bug may not surface in local development because requests are sequential and the app restarts often. It appears under load, when the singleton's captured scoped service is accessed concurrently from multiple requests.

The problematic code injects a scoped service into a singleton's constructor. The .NET container resolves the singleton once, constructs it with the first scoped instance, and then reuses that same instance for every request. The scoped service is now effectively a singleton, which breaks its contract.

data.content: A singleton that captures a scoped DbContext:

data.text: There are three safe ways to use scoped services inside a singleton: inject IServiceScopeFactory and create a scope per operation, inject an ILogger (which is designed to be a singleton), or change the lifetime of the consuming service to scoped if it does not need to be a singleton. The factory pattern is the most common fix.

data.title: Fix: create a scope per operation
data.content: Use IServiceScopeFactory to resolve scoped services inside the method instead of the constructor:

cards.description: Create a new scope inside the singleton method.

cards.description: Make the consuming service scoped if it does not need to be a singleton.
cons: Creates a new instance per request

cards.description: Inject Func<AppDbContext> and call it inside the method.

data.title: How to detect captive dependencies
data.text: Enable the .NET service provider validation warning in development. The container throws at startup when it detects a captive dependency. In production, monitor for ObjectDisposedException and cross-request data leakage as early warning signs.

data.title: What to look for in a pull request
items: Singleton constructor parameters that are registered as scoped or transient
DbContext or repository injected into a singleton
Missing IServiceScopeFactory usage in long-lived services
No using statement around a manually created scope
Comments suggesting the developer was unsure about lifetime

items.question: Is ILogger safe to inject into a singleton?
items.answer: Yes. ILogger and ILoggerFactory are designed to be singletons. They are thread-safe and do not hold request-scoped state.

items.question: Can I use a static DbContext instance?
items.answer: Never. DbContext is explicitly not thread-safe and is designed to be scoped. A static instance will cause data corruption under concurrent access.

items.question: What about IOptions<T> in a singleton?
items.answer: IOptions<T> is safe in a singleton because it is a singleton itself. IOptionsSnapshot<T> is scoped and should not be injected into singletons.

items.question: Does IServiceScopeFactory create a new scope for every call?
items.answer: Yes. Each call to CreateScope returns a new IServiceScope with its own scoped service provider. Dispose it when done.

data.title: Refactor a captive dependency
data.description: Given a singleton service that takes a scoped repository in its constructor, refactor it to use IServiceScopeFactory without changing the public API.
steps: Identify all scoped dependencies in the singleton constructor
Replace constructor injection with IServiceScopeFactory injection
Create a scope inside each method that needs the scoped service
Add using statements to dispose scopes properly
Write a test that creates multiple concurrent requests and asserts no exceptions
data.expectedOutcome: The singleton no longer holds a captive dependency. Each call gets a fresh scoped instance, and concurrent requests do not interfere with each other.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Never inject a scoped service into a singleton constructor
Use IServiceScopeFactory to create scopes inside singleton methods
Enable service provider validation at startup to catch these bugs early
Understand the lifetime of every service you consume
data.takeaway: A captive dependency is a hidden coupling between lifetimes. Fix it at construction time, not in production.
